sections.title: What the Ecommerce Website Developer Role Involves

inline: An ecommerce website developer builds and maintains the technical infrastructure of an online store. Depending on the company and platform, the role can lean front-end, back-end, or full-stack, but most ecommerce developer jobs share a common core of responsibilities.

items: Building and customizing storefronts, product pages, and checkout flows.
Integrating payment gateways, shipping providers, and third-party APIs.
Working with marketing and design teams on promotional features and A/B tests.
Monitoring performance, fixing bugs, and optimizing load times.
Maintaining security patches and platform updates.
Supporting product launches and seasonal campaigns.

blocks.text: Where ecommerce developers sit in a company

inline: In smaller companies, a single ecommerce developer often covers front-end, back-end, and platform administration. In larger companies, the role splits: front-end developers handle UX and performance, back-end developers handle integrations and data, and platform specialists handle the ecommerce engine itself. Full-stack developers bridge the two.

Ecommerce developers are not usually responsible for brand design, content writing, or SEO strategy. Those are separate roles, though developers often implement the technical side of design and SEO. If you are hiring for a broader "growth" or "web" role, that is a different job.

sections.title: How to Break Into Ecommerce Development

inline: If you are on the career side, the fastest path into ecommerce development is to pick a platform, build real stores, and learn the non-technical side of ecommerce well enough to scope work and talk to stakeholders.

Pick one platform — Shopify or WooCommerce are the most common entry points — and learn it thoroughly before branching out. A developer who knows one platform deeply is more employable than one who knows three shallowly.
Build stores you can show. A portfolio of three real ecommerce projects (even small ones) beats a certificate. Ship something that handles a real checkout, a real product catalog, and a real order.

blocks.text: Step 3: Learn the ecommerce business side

inline: The strongest ecommerce developers understand conversion, AOV, checkout friction, and the seasonal cadence of retail. That context is what separates a developer who builds stores from a developer who builds stores that sell.

blocks.text: Step 4: Contribute to open source or build a tool

inline: Contributing to a WooCommerce or Shopify open-source project, or building a small tool or app, is a strong signal to employers. It also creates a public proof of skill that is easier to verify than a resume.
Target agencies first. Agencies hire more juniors and give broader platform exposure faster than in-house roles. After two to three years at an agency, move in-house if you want stability and depth.

sections.title: Hiring for the Role: Employer Guidance

inline: If you are on the employer side and hiring an ecommerce developer, the process below avoids the most common hiring mistakes.
List the platform, the stack, and the day-to-day work. "Ecommerce developer" alone attracts generalists. A specific description attracts candidates who can actually do the job on day one.

blocks.text: Screen for platform depth, not title

inline: A candidate's title matters less than their platform depth. Ask for live stores they built, then open them on mobile and go through checkout. That test is more reliable than a resume.
A small paid task on a real piece of your store work reveals more than a technical interview. For the full process, see

faqs.q: Do I need a degree to become an ecommerce developer?
a: No. Employers care more about a live portfolio and platform depth than a degree. A strong portfolio of three real stores, plus demonstrated platform expertise, is the most common path into the role without a degree.
